newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait proposes foreign stakes in local utilities.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait proposes foreign stakes in local utilities.

text.p: A Kuwaiti draft law envisages foreign partnership in utility firms earmarked for privatisation as a move to to boost efficiency and secure the transfer of advanced technology, Kuwaiti officials said on Saturday.

One official told Reuters that the government had presented parliament with a privatisation law which, if approved, would allow global giants to take up a stake of some 20 percent stake in Kuwaiti utility firms.

He said Kuwait's telecommunications and electricity sectors were prime candidates for foreign participation, with the government continuing to hold some 25 percent and the rest to be sold off mainly to Kuwaiti and other Gulf Arab investors.
Another official said Kuwait was not opposed to foreigners holding shares in Kuwaiti firms but it was taking a gradual approach.

Officials have expressed hope parliament would pass the law this year to start the complex process of privatising heavily-subsidised utility firms, which are also used as employment centres for Kuwaiti nationals.

Parliamentary sources told Reuters that while many MPs had concerns over the possible laying off of Kuwaiti labour and price rises for basic services, the foreign partnership issue was not one of major difference with the government.
Since the start of the first phase of the privatisation plan in September 1994, Kuwait has sold stakes in 20 local firms for $2.3 billion. About 34 other firms worth some $3 billion remain.

Officials say the law that will sanction the next stage contains many ideas to tackle unemployment and concerns about the price of basic services, insisting that funds earned privatisation and Kuwait's oil wealth were sufficient to pay for generous redundancies and training to retool the Kuwaiti workforce.

Proposed solutions include granting citizens cash to cushion the rise in prices that would follow the privatisation of basic services. Some officials argue that the move would prove to be less costly than current subsidies.

The state could also tackle the sticky issue of employment by offering to pay part of the salaries of Kuwaitis employed by privatised strategic services firms on a decreasing annual scale over several years, experts said.

Some experts who are concerned with the future of the Kuwaiti workforce urged the government to grant Kuwaitis in the private sector the same social benefits that public sector employees receive to encourge their transfer.

The Kuwaiti government, which has a cradle-to-grave welfare system for its some 710,000 nationals, employs 92.7 percent of Kuwaitis in the workforce. Wages and salaries absorb about half of the $14 billion budget, officials say.
